items.stem: Priya, a sociology student, found the following figures in a report on school intake and league table position in Cairo. The report was based on 90 secondary schools. Table: percentage of pupils eligible for free school meals | 2010 | 2025. Top-third schools | 11% | 10%. Middle-third schools | 21% | 19%. Bottom-third schools | 33% | 38%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Middle-third schools between 2010 and 2025. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that marketisation has increased polarisation between schools.
items.answer: (a) 19 − 21 = -2 percentage points. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Bottom-third schools; the figure fell for Top-third schools, Middle-third schools; Bottom-third schools had the highest figure for 2025. Cream-skimming by popular schools concentrates disadvantaged pupils in less popular schools (Bartlett). Qualifications: Differences may reflect housing patterns that existed before marketisation; schools in poorer areas may still improve; free school meal eligibility is only a rough measure of disadvantage. The data also come from official statistics of 90 secondary schools in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 21 and 19; 1 mark for -2 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: A sociologist in Karachi wants to research the experiences of villagers affected by an aid project. Explain one strength and two limitations of using self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: Strength: there is no interviewer present, so interviewer bias is avoided and anonymity is easier to guarantee. Limitations: 1. pre-set answers cannot capture the subjective meanings people attach to their experiences. 2. response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative.
items.markingKey: For each of three points: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to the experiences of villagers affected by an aid project. [6]

items.stem: A sociologist in Dubai wants to research long-term effects of television viewing on attitudes to crime. Explain two limitations of using structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: 1. The fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth. 2. The interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to long-term effects of television viewing on attitudes to crime. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using content analysis to research how television news reports industrial disputes.
items.answer: Strengths: quantitative content analysis using a coding sheet can be repeated by another researcher, so it is reliable; it is cheap and the sources (newspapers, television, websites) are easy to obtain. Limitations: it shows what content contains but not how audiences interpret it; counting images or words may miss their deeper meaning and context. Theory: content analysis is favoured by positivist (quantitative content analysis) or interpretivist (qualitative content analysis) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how television news reports industrial disputes but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Mateo surveyed 400 adults about how they define religion. Table: adults agreeing (%) | Say this makes a person religious | Say this applies to them. Belief in God | 81% | 52%. Belief in a spiritual force but not God | 33% | 25%. Belong to a religious group | 63% | 33%. Practise rituals at home | 50% | 44%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Say this makes a person religious and Say this applies to them for Belief in God. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that how religion is defined affects how religious a society appears.
items.answer: (a) 52 − 81 = -29 percentage points (Say this applies to them compared with Say this makes a person religious). (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is lower for Say this applies to them than for Say this makes a person religious among Belief in God, Belief in a spiritual force but not God, Belong to a religious group, Practise rituals at home; Belief in God had the highest figure for Say this applies to them. Most people use a substantive definition (belief in God). Qualifications: Closed questions may not capture complex views; one city may be untypical; social desirability may affect answers. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 400 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 81 and 52; 1 mark for 29 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: A research team is investigating minority ethnic pupils’ experiences of school. Explain one strength and two limitations of using longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) for this research.
items.answer: Strength: they can follow children through their education into adulthood. Limitations: 1. being studied repeatedly may change participants’ behaviour. 2. sample attrition (people dropping out) can make the sample unrepresentative over time.
items.markingKey: For each of three points: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to minority ethnic pupils’ experiences of school. [6]

items.stem: A research team is investigating how newspapers report climate change. Explain two strengths of using content analysis for this research.

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using case studies to research how young people in Dubai view global brands.
items.answer: Strengths: they may use several methods, increasing validity; they give a detailed, in-depth picture of one group, institution or community. Limitations: a single case cannot show how widespread a pattern is; the researcher’s interpretation may be biased. Theory: case studies are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce mainly qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how young people in Dubai view global brands but best combined with another method such as content analysis (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: A survey of 600 adults in Kuala Lumpur produced the results below. Table: adults (%) | Women | Men. Pray at least weekly | 40% | 24%. Attend services at least monthly | 33% | 25%. Take part in New Age or holistic activities | 8% | 2%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Women and Men for Pray at least weekly. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that women are more religious than men.
items.answer: (a) 24 − 40 = -16 percentage points (Men compared with Women). (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is lower for Men than for Women among Pray at least weekly, Attend services at least monthly, Take part in New Age or holistic activities; Attend services at least monthly had the highest figure for Men. New Age emphasis on healing appeals to women. Qualifications: Self-report may differ by gender; differences vary by age and religion; men may participate in other forms; one city may be untypical. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 600 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 40 and 24; 1 mark for 16 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: An international company sells the same digital learning platform to schools in Cape Town and in forty other countries. Explain how functionalist and postmodernist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: international comparisons help societies improve their education systems and develop human capital for the global economy. Postmodernism: globalisation increases diversity and choice in education but also shows there is no single best system.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: A survey of 500 households with children in Istanbul produced the data below. Table: percentage of households in relative poverty | 2010 | 2025. Group A | 45% | 46%. Group B | 29% | 32%. Majority group | 19% | 16%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Group B between 2010 and 2025. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that material deprivation explains ethnic differences in achievement.
items.answer: (a) 32 − 29 = +3 percentage points. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Group A, Group B; the figure fell for Majority group; Group A had the highest figure for 2025. Differences in employment rates and family size. Qualifications: Some groups with high poverty rates achieve well; in-school factors and racism also matter; poverty measures may not capture wealth or support networks. The data also come from official statistics of 500 households with children in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 29 and 32; 1 mark for +3 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: A survey of 240 members of sects in Karachi was compared with census data for the city. Table: percentage in each group | Sect members | General population. Unemployed or in low-paid work | 49% | 26%. Recently moved to the city | 29% | 18%. Have a university degree | 21% | 26%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Sect members and General population for Have a university degree. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that deprivation explains why people join sects.
items.answer: (a) 26 − 21 = +5 percentage points (General population compared with Sect members). (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is higher for General population than for Sect members among Have a university degree; the figure is lower for General population than for Sect members among Unemployed or in low-paid work, Recently moved to the city. Sects attract the marginalised (Weber). Qualifications: Many sect members are not deprived; relative deprivation is hard to measure; sect members may not be representative; correlation is not causation. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 240 members in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 21 and 26; 1 mark for 5 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Exam data from Riyadh show that pupils from one migrant community achieve well above the national average, while pupils from another achieve well below it. Compare how interactionist and Marxist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Interactionism: ethnic differences are partly created in schools through teachers’ stereotypes and labels, which shape set placements and pupils’ self-concepts (Archer, Gillborn). Marxism: ethnic differences are bound up with class inequality: minority groups are over-represented in poverty and institutional racism helps reproduce disadvantage.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Hana, a sociology student, is designing a project on how teenagers interpret music videos. Explain two limitations of using field experiments for this research.
items.answer: 1. The researcher has much less control over variables than in a laboratory. 2. They are hard to repeat exactly because conditions in the real world change.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to how teenagers interpret music videos. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of structured interviews for studying religious participation in countries with different levels of competition.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; every respondent is asked the same questions in the same order, so results are standardised and reliable. Limitations: they are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid; the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying religious participation in countries with different levels of competition but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: The table shows official data on investment by TNCs in three developing countries. Table: inflows of foreign direct investment by TNCs (billion dollars) | 2005 | 2020. Country A | 11 | 25. Country B | 27 | 36. Country C | 3 | 5. (a) Calculate the change, in billion dollars, for Country A between 2005 and 2020. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that TNC investment brings development to poorer countries.
items.answer: (a) 25 − 11 = +14 billion dollars. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Country A, Country B, Country C; Country B had the highest figure for 2020. Some countries became less attractive as wages rose or instability grew. Qualifications: Investment figures do not show who benefits; profits may be repatriated; jobs may be low-paid; investment may leave quickly. The data also come from official statistics of 3 countries in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 11 and 25; 1 mark for +14 billion dollars (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: A local film industry in Nairobi struggles to compete as cinemas show mainly Hollywood films, which have much bigger marketing budgets. Compare how pluralist and Marxist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Pluralism: media success reflects audience choice in a competitive market: Hollywood dominates where audiences prefer it, while local and non-Western producers can and do compete when they meet audience demand. Marxism: global media spread Western capitalist values and consumerism, serving the interests of US-based corporations (Schiller).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: In a school in Mumbai, 80% of pupils taking computer science are boys, while 75% of those taking health and social care are girls. Explain how a radical feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Radical feminism: subject choice and the hidden curriculum reflect patriarchy: schools steer girls to lower-paid caring careers and reinforce male dominance.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using official statistics to research the amount of user-generated content on news websites.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; they are usually free and readily available, saving time and money. Limitations: they are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs; interpretivists argue they are social constructions shaped by the decisions of officials and the public. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the amount of user-generated content on news websites but best combined with another method such as content analysis (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Three groups in Karachi watch the same news report on a nurses’ strike: hospital managers say the strike is irresponsible, nurses say it is justified, and students accept that pay is low but think the strike is harmful. Suggest how a neo-Marxist sociologist might explain this.

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Cultural imperialism suggests powerful societies dominate other cultures.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. It mainly refers to Western, especially American, influence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of structured interviews for studying the role of religious leaders in a protest movement.
items.answer: Strengths: response rates are usually higher than for postal questionnaires because the interviewer is present; every respondent is asked the same questions in the same order, so results are standardised and reliable. Limitations: the interviewer’s presence may produce interviewer bias or socially desirable answers; they are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the role of religious leaders in a protest movement but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Omar is planning a study of which types of stories appear in newspapers. Explain one strength and two limitations of using content analysis for this research.
items.answer: Strength: quantitative content analysis using a coding sheet can be repeated by another researcher, so it is reliable. Limitations: 1. it shows what content contains but not how audiences interpret it. 2. coding categories reflect the researcher’s own interpretation, so different coders may disagree.
items.markingKey: For each of three points: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to which types of stories appear in newspapers. [6]

items.stem: A sociologist in Auckland wants to research how parents from different social classes choose schools. Explain two limitations of using personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) for this research.
items.answer: 1. They cannot show how common a pattern is across a society. 2. Their meaning must be interpreted by the researcher, which may introduce bias.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to how parents from different social classes choose schools. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using structured interviews to research how journalists decide what to report.
items.answer: Strengths: answers can be quantified and compared between social groups; the interviewer can explain unclear questions, so fewer answers are spoiled. Limitations: the interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour; they are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how journalists decide what to report but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]
